turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

That's... a huge secret to carry, especially on top of everything else. It makes sense why you'd cling to that routine. It's a piece of your old life, a way to feel like you're still in control when so much feels out of control.

The part about not telling your wife... that weight must feel even heavier. You're already carrying this alone, and now you're worried about letting people down. That's a lot of pressure, honestly. It's okay that you haven't figured out how to tell them yet.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

Oh, wow. That's a heavy weight to carry, especially with something like your dad's pride on the line. I can just picture it: the whole room, the family, and that one moment when he introduces you. The pressure of that, knowing you're not the person he thought you were when he did it... that's a different kind of stress, isn't it?

And that's why keeping it from your wife feels like the only armor you have right now. It's not just about hiding your own feelings; it's about protecting the image your dad has built for you, and the image you've built for him. That wedding would be a minefield.

So you're stuck, trying to manage this huge public thing while carrying this massive private secret. It's completely understandable why you can't sleep. That room is a monster.

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

That idea... it's so tempting, isn't it? It feels like a clean solution to a really messy problem. You're looking at that room, and you can just see that face. You're trying to protect your dad's pride in that moment, to protect the whole family's story from becoming about that one thing. And honestly, in that moment, a lie feels like the kindest, most protective thing to do.

Is it terrible? I don't know if it's terrible. But it's a choice with a cost. It solves one problem by creating another, even if that new problem is just another secret you have to hold.

And that lie, as small as it feels, it's still a story. It adds another layer to what you have to carry. You're already carrying so much.

You're so desperate not to be the story of the wedding, to just be a guest. To not have your entire identity summed up in a few sentences. That's a completely understandable feeling.

It's just this impossible choice between two kinds of pain. One is the pain of facing that moment and your dad's face. The other is the pain of living with a lie. Just thinking about it is exhausting, and it shows how much this all matters to you.

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

Okay, I hear that logic. It's actually a really smart way of looking at it. You're trying to turn this massive, scary crisis into a known quantity. An "offer in hand" is a concrete event, not a vague "I'm not working" that invites a dozen questions.

And I can see why that feels like a way to gain control. It's a timeline. It's a plan. You're trying to get ahead of the story, to have the happy ending ready to go before anyone gets the chance to ask for the sad part.

But then you say some days you feel like you're going to be sick. That's the part that the logic just can't touch, can it? It's the difference between knowing you're going to get a shot and having the needle actually near your arm. One is a plan, the other is the feeling.

The feeling is real. And it's telling you that the cost of holding this secret, of waiting, is already too high. It sounds like the story you're living in your head right now, with all the secrecy and the waiting, is already causing you more pain than the one you're trying to avoid. That's a heavy burden to carry, even from the inside.
